items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: Now in the middle of all this stuff Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson

ctx.x: But back in the twenties, you know Louis sang about it, pot, gage, whatever they called it that marijuana was — but that, the alcoholism wasn’t peculiar to musicians and the musicians didn’t get the rap of, I think big time — for instance like the white bands and the colored bands that were really, the black bands, colored, Jimmie Lunceford and those bands, particularly bands like Jimmie Lunceford and to a lesser extent Basie, even though these guys were free spirits, the discipline in the bands was considerable.…

fixed it so they would fire themselves, which is a great lesson in — when you have self esteem to that level — Basie was great, he was quietly running that band but he knew what was going on. So to the alcoholism you’re talking about the ones where it impacted to the point where it was messing them up would be like any other profession, you drink yourself out of a job. Of course the folklore, I mean the Charlie Parkers of the world were larger than life people. They had different physical constitution but it…
Did some of the fellas think that you needed to be high to play, to be able to keep up?
